newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lyonnaise and Suez in merger talks.
newsitem.headline: Lyonnaise and Suez in merger talks.

text.p: French conglomerates Lyonnaise des Eaux and Cie de Suez lifted a lengthy veil of silence on Friday to confirm they were in merger talks.
The companies ended over a week of frenzied stock market activity and media speculation on an alliance with a brief statement that the two boards would consider a merger project on April 11.

The joint statement said the Suez and Lyonnaise boards would meet as already planned on April 1 and April 2 respectively to approve 1996 results, and then hold special meetings on April 11 "to discuss a merger plan between the two companies."
Spokesmen at both companies declined all further comment.
However, one source close to the deal said a straight merger -- rather than a share swap -- would speed up tying the knot.
"With a share swap, we have to submit a bid, and then wait for the investors to turn in their shares. Then we have to make a minority buy-out bid. That takes time," the source said.
"With a merger, investors have no choice but to turn in their shares. If they don't agree with the merger, they can sell off their new shares afterwards," the source told Reuters.

Analysts say it makes sense to merge the two, Lyonnaise with its sprawling empire in water distribution, electricity and construction, and Suez, a conglomerate seeking a raison d'etre after selling off investment bank Indosuez and other key assets.
Such a deal would solve an identity crisis for the cash-rich Suez and could provide Lyonnaise with the resources to keep up with expanding rival Cie Generale des Eaux, they say.

A potential political obstacle to an alliance appeared to have receded on Friday when Belgian Prime Minister said he had an offer of guarantees from Suez that a deal would not hurt the independence of Belgian utility holding Tractebel.

Tractebel is 65 percent-controlled by Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB), but because SGB is itself controlled by Suez there were worries in Belgium that a merger between Lyonnaise and Suez could compromise Tractebel's position in the Belgian gas and electricity market.

"There is an approach and willingness on both sides to meet the problems raised by the (Belgian) government," Dehane told a news conference after the weekly Belgian cabinet meeting. "I am convinced these (talks) will end with an agreement."

Together, Lyonnaise and Suez would jump the French company league, probably to around tenth position in terms of market capitalisation but still behind rival utilities-to-media giant Generale des Eaux.

The firms affected by any deal through their shareholdings or involvement in the sector include a number of major players such as Generale des Eaux, which has an indirect stake in Suez through a 20 percent holding in Belgium's Electrafina.
Generale des Eaux has denied reports it would try to block a Lyonnaise/Suez alliance by launching a counter-bid for Suez.

Suez, which has sold off assets and has been shoring up its accounts after heavy losses when the property market collapsed in the early 1990s, posted a net attributable loss of 3.96 billion francs in 1995. Lyonnaise profit in the same year fell to 906 million from 1.06 billion francs.
